A reading in ten slides

Kimono

Recognised today by its T-shaped form, its characteristic sleeves and a wide sash, the obi, tied at the waist.4

On the right: Outer robe (uchikake) with mandarin oranges and folded-paper butterflies, Japan, late 18th–early 19th century. The Met, 1976.108. CC0 1.0.
Photograph, not a rendering. Full credit on slide 10.

The question

Is a kimono a garment,or a set of rules?

ANSWER A

A garment

Straight pieces cut from cloth of one standard width, with almost no waste.4 You could draw the pattern with a ruler.

ANSWER B

A set of rules

An order of dressing, a season for each pattern, a sleeve length that marks who may wear it.4

Hold both answers. Slide 10 decides.

Structure · the cut

Straight cuts,one width,almost no waste.

The bolt

Kimono cloth comes in one standard width. Cutting it gives geometric pieces with square outlines and hardly any waste.4

Sleevessode

Each sleeve is one width of fabric, attached along the selvages, the bolt’s woven edges.4 quoting 1

The front

An attached neckband runs round an open front that overlaps, always left over right.4

Not a style choice: right over left is associated with dressing the dead.4

Diagram simplified to the pieces the sources name. Real cutting layouts include further strips.

Structure · the shape

Flat on the table.Shaped only when worn.

No tucks or darts give a kimono a three-dimensional shape. Unworn, its surface is completely flat.4

In this unfitted form it is largely free of size and unisex. The fit comes from dressing, called kitsuke.4

Careful: “unisex” applies to the flat garment, “in their unfitted form”, not to how men and women wear it.4

Western sleeve

A curved armhole, cut to fit the shoulder and arm.5

Kimono sleeve

A straight, deep armhole. Western fashion borrowed the name “kimono sleeve”.5

Fabric and season

Season is written downas a rule.

Rule · when to wear a flower

Advice books remind readers to match the pattern to the season. One rule: start wearing a flower about a month before it blooms, and stop just before it does.4

Shiotsuki’s Kimono no Hon (1972) lists 390 rules on buying, choosing and wearing kimono.4

Cloth · summer gauze

The Met’s Kimono Style lists an unlined summer kimono (hito-e) of ro, a gauze-weave silk, from the 1920s–30s.2

One object label, seen as a search excerpt: it shows the practice, not a calendar.

Unlined summer kimono (hito-e), embroidered and resist-dyed silk gauze (ro). The Met, 1998.487.5. CC0 1.0.

A rule is not the same as practice: many young women in Becke’s fieldwork could not identify specific motifs.4

Kitsuke · the wearing order

“Seventy percent of what makes a kimono a kimono is how it is worn.”4

The head of a kimono company, quoted by Becke.

  1. Under-kimono first. The nagajuban goes on before anything else.4
  2. Even out the body. Towels and hip pads make a flat surface to wrap.4
  3. Wrap left over right. The reverse is for dressing the dead.4
  4. Set the hem. Straight, just above the feet; spare length folds at the waist, the ohashori.4
  5. Obi, sash cloth, cord. The obi-age finishes the top; the obi-jime cord sits mid-obi.4
  6. The knot, last. The guides end by tying the obi knot.4

The craft is straightness, alignment, no wrinkles, not symmetry: the designs are often asymmetrical. Schools issue certificates for it.4

Pattern

Where the pattern sitssays how formal it is.

Motifs
CHERRY · sakuraWISTERIA · fujiPEONY · botanCHRYSANTHEMUM · kiku

Classic coming-of-age furisode mostly carry late-winter and spring flowers (camellia, plum, cherry, peony, wisteria, narcissus) to suit a January ceremony.4 The chrysanthemum appears mainly as a symbol of the nation and the imperial house.4

Rules bend: some modern furisode use peonies, roses and lilies rather than seasonal flowers.4

Placement

Eba-moyō, ceremonial. One continuous, asymmetrical design, gathered below the obi and on the left shoulder.4

Komon, less formal. Small motifs repeated all over the garment.45

The long-sleeved furisode is ceremonial wear, mainly for unmarried women.4 From the early 1600s printed pattern books (hinagata-bon) showed buyers the designs on offer.4

Kosode, Edo period, 18th century: fence, cherry, chrysanthemum and flower cart. Tokyo National Museum. Photo: Daderot. CC0 1.0.

History

The word is newerthan the garment.

“Kimono”, from kirumono, “a thing to wear”, came into wide use only in the Meiji period; before that each garment type had its own name.4

Tamamura Kōzaburō, shop for kimono fabrics, c. 1880. Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe, F 53. CC0 1.0.

Kosode
BEFORE THE NAME

The kosode is the precursor of the modern kimono.5

Edo
FROM THE EARLY 1600S

Merchants dress lavishly despite repeated sumptuary laws; pattern books sell made-to-order designs.4

Meiji
1868–1912

Dress splits into wafuku and yōfuku, Japanese and Western; kimono becomes national costume. Men largely give it up.4

Post-war
PEAK REVENUE 1981

Most people stop wearing it; kimono turns to ritual occasions. Sales fall after the early-1990s bubble.4

Now
2000S ON · AND ABROAD

Vintage kimono revive it as casual fashion.4 Abroad, its flat, rectangular cut fed Poiret, Vionnet and Miyake.5

Decline is post-war, not the whole century: Taishō-era (1912–1926) kimono were still fashionable and modern.4

Kusakabe Kimbei, Greeting (studio no. 400), hand-coloured albumen print, c. 1880s–1890s. Public domain (PD-old).

Body language

The rules continueafter dressing.

Moving

Furisode manners pages teach how to move when walking, sitting down, climbing stairs and getting in and out of a car.4

Bowing

Correct bowing is taught as kata, proper form, in etiquette classes and school demonstrations.4

Letting the collar fall low at the back (nukiemon) was fashionable around 1907.5 Dalby advises a young woman to wear it “demurely close to her nape”.4 quoting 1

Taught, not described: the sources say these moves are taught but do not spell them out, so none are drawn.

The answer

Both.

The garment

is simple.

Straight pieces of one standard width, sewn flat, largely free of size.4

The meaning

is made by rules.

Kitsuke sets order and shape; season, placement and sleeve length code the occasion and the wearer.4

Garment or rules was the wrong cut: the cloth is the canvas, kitsuke and formality coding are what it says.
